description_full: Boyd Gaming Corporation, together with its subsidiaries, operates as a multi-jurisdictional gaming company in the United States and Canada. The company operates through Las Vegas Locals, Downtown Las Vegas, Midwest & South, and Online segments. It owns and operates casinos; Boyd Interactive, an online casino gaming business; and a travel agency. The company was formerly known as The Boyd Group and changed its name to Boyd Gaming Corporation in April 1993. Boyd Gaming Corporation was founded in 1975 and is headquartered in Las Vegas, Nevada.

culture_narrative: Employs approximately 16K people. Revenue per employee of $256K ranks in the below the sector median among Consumer Cyclical peers. Each employee generates $24K of free cash flow annually. Stock-based compensation of $2K per employee reflects an ownership culture. CEO compensation is 22× revenue per employee (reasonable relative to workforce productivity). Governance score flags moderate compensation governance risk (5/10).
financial_summary: Boyd Gaming Corporation is a mid-cap consumer cyclical business with a $5.4B market cap on $4.1B of annual revenue.
The top line has compounded at +5% over the past three years and +6% annually across the full decade, which puts it in mature, slow-growth territory.
Returns on capital run at 16% against a 8% cost of capital, a 8-point spread that creates value, though narrow enough that competitive pressure could close it.

The business throws off $388M in free cash flow — roughly 9 cents on every revenue dollar, which is the owner-earnings figure that actually belongs to shareholders. Cash conversion is thin at 0.53×, however, which raises the oldest question in analysis: are these earnings backed by cash?.
Accruals are elevated at +13.2% of assets, and Sloan showed firms building earnings through accruals rather than cash systematically underperform.
On the balance sheet, leverage is comfortably conservative at 1.6× net debt/EBITDA, and interest coverage runs at 4.7×.

Management returns a meaningful 15.5% of market cap to owners through dividends and buybacks, a strong signal of disciplined capital allocation, and insiders hold 33% of the shares, so management thinks like owners because it is one — the strongest alignment there is, and within its sector the business captures 2.2× its fair share of profits, a structural advantage visible in the numbers.

sect: Its 18% operating margin runs 11pp above the Consumer Cyclical median (8%), a real cost or pricing edge over peers.
It captures 2.22x its revenue share in sector profits, taking a disproportionate slice of the profit pool.
Over five years it has been gaining share of the sector profit pool (+90.6% a year).
The sector is fragmented and competitive (HHI 0.03 across 377 companies in the universe; the top four hold 26% of revenue), so pricing power is hard to come by.
mkt: The shares have drifted lower, down 11% over the past year excluding the latest month.
The price sits mid-way through its 52-week range, 16% below the high.
With annualised volatility of 26% and a beta of 0.92, it moves roughly with the market, though its beta has shifted (1y 0.01 vs 5y 0.91), so read it loosely.
About $73.4M trades a day, enough to build a position.
In past sell-offs it fell 77% in the 2020 crash, 35% in the 2022 bear market and 91% in 2008.
val: The price sits above its DCF fair value of $37.27 (margin of safety -105%), so there is no valuation cushion.
The fair-value models disagree (dispersion 72%), and the Monte Carlo range runs $21.81 to $60.03 (P10-P90), so treat the estimate as noisy.
On multiples it looks cheap against Consumer Cyclical peers: P/E 11.2 vs 19.3 and EV/EBITDA 7.2 vs 11.2 (sector median).
Against its own history it is dear: the EBIT multiple sits 46% above its 10-year median.
Earnings yields are attractive: an FCF yield of 7.2% (above the risk-free rate) and an EBIT/EV of 8.9% (vs the 8% bar).
The 16 covering analysts target $87.44 on average, 14% above the price, well away from the model's fair value.
prof: ROIC of 16% clears the cost of capital of 8.1% by 8pp, the mark of a value creator; returns have swung a lot from year to year (CV 1.01).
It converts 9% of revenue into free cash flow.
Earnings quality is a concern: cash conversion of only 0.53x and high accruals (+13.2% of assets).
ROE of 71% comes mostly from margins and asset turnover rather than leverage (2.5x equity multiplier).
It spends 0.8% of revenue on stock compensation.
hlth: Leverage is moderate at 1.6x net debt to EBITDA ($354.2M of cash against $2.0B of debt), above the 1.5x gate, with interest covered 4.7x.
The current ratio of 0.54 means short-term liabilities exceed current assets.
growth: Revenue has compounded at 4.8% over 3 years, 13.4% over 5 years and 6.4% over 10 years, so growth is decelerating, and it has been lumpy (year-to-year swings of 20%).
Net reinvestment is nil (capex and working capital no more than cover depreciation), so fundamental growth is near zero.
Free cash flow has compounded 27.8% a year over five years.
Capex runs 1.9x depreciation (14.4% of sales), so it is building capacity for future growth.
Its Rule of 40 score is 22, below the 40 that marks a healthy growth business.
It has beaten earnings estimates by 3.2% on average.
own: Insiders own 32.9%, meaningful skin in the game, and institutions hold 78%.
Insiders have only sold over the past year (9 sales, net $22.3M sold).
It returns 15.5% a year to shareholders (14.4% in buybacks and 1.0% in dividends).
The share count has shrunk 8.5% a year over five years, steadily raising each holder's stake.
people: With about 16,009 employees, each generates about $256K of revenue, 0.7x the Consumer Cyclical median, and productivity has risen 4.1% a year.
That works out to $24K of free cash flow per employee.
CEO pay is $5.6M (22x revenue per employee).
